title: Plus Code Finder: Addresses Without Streets
description: Find the Plus Code for any coordinates with the Plus Code Finder — Google's open location codes, full and short forms explained. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, Times Square's full Plus Code is 87G8Q257+6Q — an address for the crossroads computed from its coordinates alone, no street database consulted.
quick_answer: The Plus Code Finder gives the Plus Code (Open Location Code) for any latitude and longitude, and converts codes back to the coordinates they name. Enter a point and read its code — the open address system Google built for places with no street address.

use_cases.title: Checking a code from the wild

body.t: Found a code on a sign or listing? Decode it here and see the square it names before trusting it.
Google's own headquarters encodes to 849VCWC8+R9 — the published reference example this encoder's arithmetic reproduces exactly. Times Square is 87G8Q257+6Q; the Eiffel Tower, 8FW4V75V+9Q.

examples.label: Example · Short codes need a town

body.t: Near a known place, the code shortens: Q257+6Q works with 'New York' because the first characters are implied by locality. Short codes are local dialect; full codes are the universal language.

popular_table.note: The alphabet omits vowels and look-alikes (20 safe characters), so codes cannot spell words or be misread at a glance. The system is open and offline-computable — no server decides your address.

faq: Nobody centrally — the Open Location Code is an open standard (created at Google Zurich, now community-stewarded). Any app can compute codes offline, including this one.
Full codes work worldwide with no context. Short codes drop the area prefix and need a reference locality ('Q257+6Q, New York') — the finder produces full codes you can shorten safely.
About 14 metres square at the equator, narrowing in longitude toward the poles — precisely, 0.000125 degrees per side at the final pair's resolution.
Can I navigate to a code?
Google Maps and many other apps accept Plus Codes in search. The code pasted there lands on the cell this finder shows.
Codes for places with no name?
That is the point of the system — oceans aside, every square metre of land can carry a code whether or not anyone named it.
No — a code is pure arithmetic on coordinates. It names the same cell forever.
Possible (each extra grid character refines further), but 11 already beats consumer GPS accuracy; more characters are ceremony.
